The `gridcalc` package in /app evaluates spreadsheet-style sheets of cells and formulas into JSON documents, and it has bugs. Some of its unit tests fail. From /app, run them with:

    python -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

Fix the package code under /app/gridcalc so that it follows the rules in /app/docs (start with /app/docs/overview.md). Those rules are not the ones of any spreadsheet program you may know; where they differ, the docs decide. Passing the unit tests is not enough: the package will also be run on other sheets, and every document it writes must follow the docs. Do not change anything under /app/tests, /app/data or /app/docs.

When you are done, write /app/STATUS.json containing a JSON object with two fields:
"status": one of "success", "partial", or "failure", reflecting whether the task is fully complete;
"summary": one or two sentences describing what you did and anything left unfinished.

This note covers the text format of `DATA/sheets/<id>.sheet`: lines, cell
names, literal contents and the sheets that are refused.

## 1. Lines

1.1 A sheet file is read line by line. Leading and trailing spaces and tabs of
a line are ignored.

1.2 A line that is empty after that is skipped. A line whose first character
is `#` is a comment and is skipped.

1.3 Every other line defines one cell:

    CELL: CONTENT

`CELL` is a cell name (section 2). Spaces or tabs may stand between the name
and the colon. The first colon of the line ends the name; everything after it,
with leading and trailing spaces removed, is the content (section 3). A colon
inside the content, as in a range `A1:B3`, is part of the content.

1.4 The order of the lines does not matter. A formula may name a cell that is
defined further down the file.

## 2. Cell names

2.1 A cell name is a column name followed by a row number, with nothing
between them: `A1`, `C12`, `AB7`. Column and row are those of `formulas.md`
section 4. Letters may be written in either case; `ab7` is the cell `AB7`.

2.2 A sheet file names a cell without `$` signs. `$A$1` is not a cell name
here (it is a valid reference inside a formula).

2.3 The row number may have leading zeros; `A07` is the cell `A7`.

## 3. Contents

3.1 A content that starts with `=` is a formula. The whole content, including
the `=`, is the formula text. The text after `=` is read by `formulas.md`.

3.2 Any other content is a literal. It is read in this order:

1. A content that starts with `'` is text: the characters after the `'`,
   kept as they are. `'42` is the text `42`, not a number; `'TRUE` is the
   text `TRUE`.
2. A content that is a number as `values.md` 2.3 defines it is that number:
   `12`, `-4`, `0.25`, `.5`, `1.5e3`, `2E-2`.
3. `TRUE` and `FALSE`, in any case, are booleans.
4. Anything else is text, as written: `apple`, `Birch 2`, `#DIV/0!`.

3.3 A literal is never evaluated. The content `1+1` is the text `1+1`.

## 4. What a sheet defines

4.1 The cells a sheet defines are exactly the cells its lines name. Every
other cell of the grid is undefined and reads as empty (`values.md` 2.5).

4.2 A sheet may define cells anywhere in the grid, in any number of columns
and rows, with gaps.

## 5. Refused sheets

5.1 A sheet is refused, as a whole, when its file:

- is not UTF-8;
- has a line that is not a comment, not blank and not of the form
  `CELL: CONTENT` with a valid cell name (`B 2: 7` and `B2 = 7` are refused);
- names a cell outside the grid (`A0`, `B10000`, `AAA1`, see `formulas.md`
  4.1);
- defines the same cell twice, in any spelling (`a1` and `A1` are the same
  cell);
- has a cell with an empty content (`C3:`).

5.2 A refused sheet gets no document. It is listed in `errors.json` with the
error class `SheetError` (`output.md` section 4).

5.3 A formula that cannot be read is not a reason to refuse a sheet. Its cell
takes the value `#PARSE!` (`formulas.md` 2.6).
# Formulas

parentheses.

1.2 Spaces and tabs between tokens are ignored. They are never needed, except
inside strings, where they are kept.

    OUT/errors.json        the sheets that were refused

2.1 An evaluated document is a JSON object with these keys, in this order:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `sheet` | the sheet id |
| `cells` | one object per cell the sheet defines |

(`formulas.md` 4.4): `A9` comes before `A10`, and `Z3` before `AA1`.

2.3 Each cell object has these keys, in this order:

| Key | Value |
|---|---|
| `cell` | the cell name, upper case, without `$` |
| `type` | `number`, `text`, `bool` or `error`, the kind of the cell's value |
| `value` | the value, written as in 2.4 |
| `formula` | formula cells only: the formula text as written in the sheet, from its `=` |
| `refs` | formula cells only: the refs listing (2.5) |

- entries are in cell order of their first corner, then of their second

function. Function names are not case-sensitive: `sum(A1:A3)` is

## 1. Calls and arguments

1.1 A call is a name, `(`, arguments separated by commas, and `)`. A call to a
name that is not in this note evaluates to `#NAME?` and its arguments are not
evaluated. A call with fewer or more arguments than the function takes
evaluates to `#VALUE!`.

1.2 **Reference arguments.** An argument written as a single reference or as
a range, alone or inside parentheses, is a reference argument. Its cells are:

- for a single reference, that one cell, whose value is empty when the sheet
  does not define it;
- for a range, the cells the sheet defines inside the rectangle, in cell order
  (`formulas.md` 4.4). Undefined cells of a range are not part of it.

Any other argument, such as `A1+0`, `"4"` or `IF(B1, A1, A2)`, is an
expression argument. It has one value.

1.3 **Errors.** For every function except `COUNT`, `IF` and `IFERROR`, the
expression arguments are evaluated first, in order, and the first one whose
value is an error value is the result of the call. Error values inside
reference arguments are handled by each function, as stated below. `COUNT`
never passes an error on. `IF` and `IFERROR` evaluate only what they use
(section 6).

1.4 A function that reads one value from an argument (`ROUND`, `ABS`, `LEN`,
`NOT`, the condition of `IF`) reads the value of a single reference as it is;
a range there gives `#VALUE!`.

- a reference argument contributes those of its cells that are numbers. Cells

- an expression argument is read as a number (`values.md` 2.1): `TRUE` gives
  1, `"4"` gives 4, and `"x"` gives `#VALUE!`, which is the result of the

Arguments are taken in order, so an error value in an earlier argument wins.

2.2 `SUM` adds the numbers; with none it is 0. `AVERAGE` divides their sum by

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Token:
    kind: str  # num, str, ref, name or op
    text: str


def _string(text: str, i: int) -> tuple[str, int]:
    """The value of the string literal that opens at text[i], and the index after it."""

            raise FormulaError("unterminated string")
